objection.evidence:
The success criteria require that the input "must not be modified", but merge_intervals mutates the caller's data in two ways.

intervals.py line 2 sorts the caller's list in place (`intervals.sort(...)`), and the merged result is written back into the caller's own inner lists (`merged[-1][1] = max(...)` where `merged[-1]` is the caller's list object, since `merged.append(iv)` appends the original object rather than a copy).

Reproduction (script repro.py run against the deliverable, exit code 0):
1) Ordering destroyed:
   inp = [[8,10],[1,3],[2,6]]; out = merge_intervals(inp)
   -> returned [[1,6],[8,10]] but inp is now [[1,6],[2,6],[8,10]] instead of [[8,10],[1,3],[2,6]]  => "input modified? True"
2) Caller's inner lists mutated:
   a=[1,4]; b=[4,5]; merge_intervals([a,b])
   -> returned [[1,5]]; a is now [1,5] (was [1,4]); and out[0] is a (returned list aliases the caller's lists).

Also confirmed by unittest (test_review.py, run via run_unit_tests): test_input_not_modified_unsorted and test_input_not_modified_identity_of_result both FAIL (exit code 1), while the public-example tests pass. The public test only checks return values on already-safe inputs, so it does not cover this requirement.

Fix: sort a copy and copy each interval before mutating, e.g.
   items = sorted(intervals, key=lambda iv: iv[0])
   ... merged.append([iv[0], iv[1]]) / merged[-1][1] = max(...)
(Secondary robustness note, same root cause: a tuple/iterator input raises AttributeError: 'tuple' object has no attribute 'sort'; `sorted()` would also fix that.)

objection.evidence: duration.py never enforces the required unit order or the "each unit at most once" rule. It collects all `(\d+)([hms])` matches and only checks that they concatenate back to the (stripped) input, so wrong-order and repeated-unit strings are silently accepted instead of raising ValueError: parse_duration("1s5m") -> 301, parse_duration("5m1h") -> 3900, parse_duration("1h1h") -> 7200, parse_duration("30s30s") -> 60, parse_duration("1h5m5m") -> 4200, parse_duration("1m1s1m") -> 121. The success criteria state units must appear at most once and in h, m, s order, and that wrong order / repeated units must raise ValueError. test_order_and_repeats.py reproduces this: `python -m unittest discover -s /work` reports 3 failures (ValueError not raised) while the valid-input tests pass.

reviewer_verdict.summary: duration.py handles valid durations, whitespace stripping, and unknown-unit/empty rejection correctly, but it does not enforce two explicit success criteria: units must appear at most once and in h, m, s order. Because it only verifies that the regex matches reconstruct the input string, wrong-order and repeated-unit inputs are accepted (e.g. "1s5m" -> 301, "5m1h" -> 3900, "1h1h" -> 7200, "30s30s" -> 60, "1m1s1m" -> 121) instead of raising ValueError. I filed a counterexample (test_order_and_repeats.py) which fails 3 tests under `python -m unittest discover -s /work`, while the public tests and valid-input cases pass. Verdict: defective.

duration.py implements parse_duration correctly against every part of the success criteria. The anchored regex `(?:(\d+)h)?(?:(\d+)m)?(?:(\d+)s)?` with fullmatch enforces: each of h/m/s at most once, strictly in h→m→s order, digits required before each unit, and at least one group present (empty string and whitespace-only rejected). Surrounding whitespace is stripped. An exhaustive differential test against an independent reference over 579,195 generated inputs (alphabet hms015 .-+Hdx_, lengths 0-5) found zero mismatches in accept/reject decisions or computed second counts. Targeted tests confirmed the spec examples (2h=7200, 45s=45, 1h5m10s=3910, 90m=5400, 1h30m=5400) and that empty, unknown units (1d, 5x, 1H), wrong order (10s5m, 5m1h, 3h10s5m), repeated units (1h1h, 90m90m), bare units (h), internal whitespace (1h 30m), signed/decimal/exponent numbers (-5m, 1.5h, 1e3s), trailing junk (1h5m10s2) and non-string inputs all raise ValueError. No catastrophic backtracking (200k-char inputs rejected in ~4ms); all error paths raise ValueError, never another exception type. Two benign quirks observed but not spec violations: \d also matches non-ASCII decimal digits (e.g. '١٢h' -> 43200, consistent value) and strip() also removes Unicode whitespace such as \xa0 — the criteria only list empty/unknown units/wrong order/repeated units as error cases. Public test passes. No grounds for objection.

Verified with the public test plus 11 additional tests I wrote (empty, single, duplicate, negative, nested, unsorted, tuple inputs, aliasing/mutation checks, and 500 randomized inputs compared against an independent brute-force reference) — all 12 tests pass under `python -m unittest discover -s /work`. objection.evidence:
duration.py does not enforce the "each unit at most once and in h,m,s order" rule. It uses re.findall(r"(\d+)([hms])") and only checks that the concatenation of the matched pieces equals the (stripped) input, so any permutation/repetition of units is accepted and summed instead of raising ValueError.

Reproduced (Python 3, /work):
  parse_duration("1h1h")   -> 7200   (expected ValueError: repeated unit 'h')
  parse_duration("2m2m")   -> 240    (expected ValueError: repeated unit 'm')
  parse_duration("1h30m1h")-> 9030   (expected ValueError)
  parse_duration("5m1h")   -> 3900   (expected ValueError: wrong order)
  parse_duration("10s1h")  -> 3610   (expected ValueError: wrong order)
  parse_duration("1s5m")   -> 301    (expected ValueError: wrong order)

The public test (test_public.py) passes, but a regression test file I added (test_hidden_repro.py, run via run_unit_tests) fails: "AssertionError: ValueError not raised : 1h1h" and "... : 5m1h". So hidden tests covering repeated units and wrong ordering would fail. reviewer_verdict.summary: duration.py handles the valid-format cases and whitespace correctly (e.g. "2h"->7200, "1h5m10s"->3910, "  1h30m  "->5400, and rejects "", "abc", "5x", "1h 30m", "-1h", "1H"), and test_public.py passes. duration.py implements parse_duration correctly per the success criteria. The anchored fullmatch regex enforces the h/m/s order with each unit at most once, requires a digit group before each unit, and the explicit checks reject empty/whitespace-only input. Differential testing against an independent strict reference (111k exhaustive ASCII cases up to length 4, 288k random fuzz cases up to length 12, 96k exhaustive cases at lengths 5–7) produced zero behavioural differences; all valid examples ('2h', '45s', '1h5m10s', '90m', '1h30m', whitespace-padded variants) return the right int seconds, and all invalid forms (empty, 'abc', '5x', '5m1h', '10s5m', '1h1m', '1h 30m', '-1h', '1.5h', '2H', bare 'h', '1hm') raise ValueError. Public tests pass via unittest discovery, and there is no catastrophic backtracking. The only nuance is that Unicode decimal digits (e.g. '١h') are accepted since \d/int are Unicode-aware; the criteria do not restrict digits to ASCII and this is not among the enumerated error cases, so it is not a concrete defect. objection.evidence:
Polish letter ł is not transliterated — it is silently deleted, splitting the word. slugify.py only strips Unicode combining marks (category "Mn") after NFKD, but "ł"/"Ł" do NOT decompose under NFKD (unicodedata.normalize("NFKD","ł") == "ł", category "Ll"), so they fall into the `else: gap = True` branch and act as word separators instead of becoming "l".

Reproduction (run in the sandbox against /work/slugify.py):
  slugify("Łódź, Polska")  -> 'odz-polska'   (expected 'lodz-polska')
  slugify("żółw")          -> 'zo-w'         (expected 'zolw')
  slugify("Żółw Łamie Żołądź") -> 'zo-w-amie-zo-adz' (expected 'zolw-lamie-zoladz')
  slugify("Ł")             -> ''             (expected 'l')

The success criteria explicitly require transliteration of "Polish letters such as ł, ą, ż". ą/ż work (they decompose), but ł does not, so hidden tests covering ł will fail. A repro unittest is saved as test_polish_criteria.py in the review folder; `python -m unittest discover -s /work` exits 1 with AssertionError: 'odz-polska' != 'lodz-polska'.

Fix: apply an explicit transliteration map for non-decomposing letters (e.g. str.maketrans for ł→l, Ł→L, ß→ss, ø→o, đ→d, æ→ae, þ→th, ð→d, ŧ→t, ħ→h, ŋ→n, ı→i) before/after NFKD stripping. (Related side effects of the same design: 'Æon' -> 'on', 'Đorđe' -> 'or-e', 'straße' -> 'stra-e', and NFKD compatibility folding turns '½ cup' into '1-2-cup'.)

reviewer_verdict.summary:
The deliverable passes the public/visible tests (lowercase ASCII, single hyphens, no leading/trailing '-', NFKD combining-mark stripping handles ą, ż, é, ñ, ş, etc.), but it fails an explicit part of the success criteria: Polish ł/Ł are not transliterated.

slugify.py relies solely on unicodedata.normalize("NFKD", ...) plus removal of combining marks (category "Mn"). "ł"/"Ł" have no NFKD decomposition (they stay category Ll/Lu), so they hit the `else: gap = True` branch and are treated as word separators — i.e. deleted and the word split:
  slugify("Łódź, Polska") -> 'odz-polska' (expected 'lodz-polska')
  slugify("żółw") -> 'zo-w' (expected 'zolw')
  slugify("Żółw Łamie Żołądź") -> 'zo-w-amie-zo-adz' (expected 'zolw-lamie-zoladz')
  slugify("Ł") -> '' (expected 'l')

Reproduced with a repro unittest (test_polish_criteria.py) in the review folder; `run_unit_tests` exits 1 with AssertionError: 'odz-polska' != 'lodz-polska'. Hidden tests that mention Polish letters (the criteria name ł explicitly) would fail.

Same root cause produces other lost letters: 'Æon' -> 'on', 'Đorđe' -> 'or-e', 'Çağrı' -> 'cagr' (ı dropped), 'straße' -> 'stra-e'. NFKD also compatibility-folds non-letters, e.g. '½ cup' -> '1-2-cup'. Fix: add an explicit transliteration table (ł→l, Ø→o, ß→ss, æ→ae, đ→d, ı→i, ...) applied before the ASCII filter. Objection filed (claim 6bd584703e07d985c6d4e8af3fafa97785af667c35877ba14a961bb9d75d6958).

Row 7 of dates.csv is wrong. Sentence 7 in sentences.txt reads "Spotkanie zarządu odbędzie się 11 lipca 2023 r. w sali 204." — "11 lipca 2023" (lipiec = July, month 7) must be encoded as 2023-07-11, but dates.csv contains "7,2023-06-11" (month 06 = June/"czerwca"). All other 11 rows are correct, the header is "id,date", and there are exactly 12 rows with ids 1..12, so only this row violates the "all rows must be correct" criterion.

Reproduction: run an independent extraction of the Polish month names from sentences.txt and compare to dates.csv (script check3.py in this review folder, executed via run_python). Output:
  header: ['id', 'date'] nrows: 12
  ... 11 rows OK ...
  7 csv= 2023-06-11 expected= 2023-07-11 MISMATCH
  mismatches: [('7', '2023-06-11', '2023-07-11')]
A unittest version (test_review.py) also fails: AssertionError: '2023-06-11' != '2023-07-11' : sentence 7.

The public test (test_public.py) passes because it only checks the header, id sequence, and the YYYY-MM-DD regex — it never validates the actual date values, so its passing does not establish correctness.

reviewer_verdict.summary: dates.csv has the correct structure (header "id,date", 12 rows, ids 1–12, all values matching YYYY-MM-DD), and 11 of 12 dates are correct. However, row 7 is wrong: sentence 7 says "11 lipca 2023" (July = month 07), so the correct ISO date is 2023-07-11, but the CSV contains 2023-06-11. I verified this with an independent month-name extraction script (check3.py) and a unittest (test_review.py), both of which flag only row 7. The public test passes because it validates only format/ids, not date values, so it cannot detect this error. Objection filed against the claim.

invoices.csv meets all success criteria. Header is exactly invoice_no,date,vendor,total with 10 data rows. An independent parser of invoices.txt (handling ISO, DD.MM.YYYY, and "D Month YYYY" dates; and totals with comma decimals, space/point thousands separators, and leading/trailing PLN/zł currency) reproduces all 10 rows exactly: 110.87, 416.74, 917.61, 1613.48, 2504.35, 3590.22, 4871.09, 6346.96, 8017.83, 9883.70 — all with two decimals and a dot, no currency or thousands separators. All dates are valid ISO YYYY-MM-DD. Vendor names are byte-identical to the source Seller: lines (Polish/Latin-Extended characters preserved, no quoting required). File is UTF-8 with no BOM, no CR/control characters, and no unaccounted content in the source. The public test also passes. No defects found; no objection raised.

objection.evidence: The implementation only strips combining marks after NFKD and keeps characters that are already ASCII alnum. Characters with no NFKD decomposition into ASCII (category Ll/Lu, so not stripped as marks and not ASCII, so not kept) are silently DELETED rather than transliterated. The success criteria explicitly require Polish letters such as ł to be transliterated, but NFKD leaves 'ł'/'Ł' unchanged, so they fall into the "else" branch and vanish (acting as word separators). Observed: slugify("ł") == "" (expected "l"), slugify("Łódź") == "odz" (expected "lodz"), slugify("Łódź, Polska") == "odz-polska" (expected "lodz-polska"), slugify("Żółw Ąż") == "zo-w-az" (expected "zolw-az"). Same class of bug for đ/ø/æ/ß/þ/ð/ŧ/ħ and Cyrillic/Greek (e.g. slugify("Grüße")=="gru-e", slugify("Straße")=="stra-e", slugify("Æon Ørsted")=="on-rsted"), i.e. letters are dropped instead of transliterated, and hidden tests that name Polish letters (ł is called out in the criteria) will fail. test_public.py passes only because it contains no non-ASCII input. Counterexample test test_polish.py fails on the deliverable (2 failures) while keeping the public examples passing; it needs no network/3rd-party libs and only asserts the documented transliteration of ł/Ł/Ż/Ą/ż.

reviewer_verdict.summary: The deliverable fails a requirement stated explicitly in the success criteria: transliteration of Polish letters such as ł. slugify() only strips combining marks after NFKD normalization and keeps ASCII alphanumerics; any non-ASCII letter with no ASCII decomposition is silently deleted (treated as a word separator) instead of transliterated. Concrete failures: slugify("ł") == "" (expected "l"), slugify("Łódź") == "odz" (expected "lodz"), slugify("Łódź, Polska") == "odz-polska", slugify("Żółw Ąż") == "zo-w-az" (expected "zolw-az"). The same defect affects other non-decomposable letters (đ, ø, æ, ß, þ, ð, ŧ, ħ — e.g. "Grüße" -> "gru-e", "Straße" -> "stra-e", "Æon Ørsted" -> "on-rsted") and non-Latin scripts. test_public.py passes only because it contains no non-ASCII input. I filed a counterexample (test_polish.py) asserting the documented transliteration of ł/Ł/Ż/Ą/ż plus the public examples; it fails on the deliverable (2 failures) under `python -m unittest discover -s /work`.
